reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, the authors continue their longstanding strong work of using advanced multiome computational genomic tools with mouse and human genetics to elucidate the cell fate of SMC and their contribution to atherosclerosis progression. Here, the authors present a comprehensive single cell transcriptomic and epigenomic analysis of SMC populations and apply probabilistic Waddington Optimal transport (WOT) modeling across a timecourse of atherosclerosis progression (in a mouse ApoE KO model) to define dynamic SMC cell states and trajectories. By integrating scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq over time, with many more timepoints than most studies, they are able to infer a higher resolution TF regulon network to predict the top drivers of SMC phenotypic switching (SMC types, n=3) to fibromyocyte (FMC types, n=2) and to chondromyocytes (CMC). Furthermore, they use their previous model, Tcf21 KO, to gain further insight as to the changes in SMC transdifferentiation in this current work and to validate their in-silico TF perturbation computational predictions. Importantly, they integrated human CAD GWAS studies to associate changes in SMC subpopulations and cell states with disease risk in humans. Overall, in comparison to their previous work in Sharma, et al, ATVB, 2024, they now present a deeper genomic, transcriptional, and regulatory view rather than descriptive model of SMC phenotypic switching linked to human disease. This new work is technically rigorous and leverages multiome single cell sequencing data with advanced computational analysis to provide new regulatory insights into the relationship between SMC phenotypic switching and CAD.
Major Points:
• The detailed time course, computational rigor and the use of Tcf21 KO data (an established CAD gene already well studied by this group) to probe the models are strengths. Yet the reliance alone on Tcf21 as the genetic probe has limitations and reduces the novelty given how much work this group has already done on Tcf21 KO mouse models and Tcf21 human genetics. And, despite the deep dive with multiple time points and integrated computational multi-omics approaches, the inferences are confusing in places. Based on human genetics and mouse genetic models prior work infers that TCF21 may serve a protective role in atherosclerosis. This serves as a grounding for interpretation of cell states, trajectories and their regulation and their function in disease. Yet, Tcf21 is found to regulate (increase) FMC cell state – inferred as protective - and also regulate (increase) CMCs - proposed to be harmful. Based on human genetics, the authors interpret the important disease related cell regulation as FMC increase and the inferred Tcf21-mediated CMC increase to be a downstream mass effect that is not important (not harmful) but there is no direct data to support that conclusion. Similarly, the authors provide evidence that FMC1 and FMC2 can be terminal cell states but that some FMCs can transition to more harmful CMC… yet it is completely unclear what might regulate the transition or lack of transition of FMC types to CMCs – which appears to be an important cellular functional event in disease. The authors should be more circumspect in their interpretation and interrogate more comprehensively these contradictions in their data. Ideally, they would interrogate separate data (even if limited and public) for an independent and opposing key regulator of SMC phenotype switching e.g., Klf4.
• With respect to some subset of FMC1 and FMC2 populations being terminally differentiated based on data at 16 weeks of western diet (WD), more temporal data should be added especially as 16 weeks WD may not capture the complexity of later lesions and human disease. It is important to include a longer timepoint on WD, ~ 20 or 26 weeks, to determine if this holds true. Furthermore, this would also better elucidate the trajectory of CMC population with atherosclerosis progression and more advanced disease.
• The authors use WOT algorithm that was initially developed by Eric Lander’s and Aviv Regev’s labs to improve upon already available methods for cell trajectory or lineage inferring across developing tissues. However, all these methods, including the one in this manuscript, lacks the cellular resolution to accurately infer lineage tracing, specially for rarer populations. This seems evident by the apparent lack of origin of FMC2 subcluster at the earlier timepoints (~ 5 Wk). While the Sankey representation of inferred transition of state in Fig 3D clearly shows the transition SMC2 -> FMC1 -> FMC2 or SMC2 -> FMC2 in the later timepoints, it seems to have a problem inferring transition state changes for FMC2 at 5 wk. A similar issue is encountered with CMC population in the Tcf21 KO at 12 and 16 wks. The authors must comment about the temporal and cellular resolution limits of this approach and strategies to possibly improve it (i.e. adding timepoints in between?).
• In this context, it is also notable that the authors appear to use a more stringent transcript threshold than their prior work (Cheng et al., Nat Card Res. 2022 and Sharma et al., 2024) and this may miss rarer smaller clusters down the lineage lines. Indeed, In Cheng et al., Nat Card Res. 2022, the authors previously identified, albeit at a lower resolution, a smaller R-SMC cluster located in the basal plaque and primarily identified by their high Mmp3 expression, but distinct from SMC, FMC and CMC, and they hypothesized that these derived from FMC by pseudotime analysis with Slingshot. What happened to this SMC subcluster? Was it integrated into the new CMC cluster or was it not detected on this dataset?
• The authors should show the actual percentage change in FMC2 population between control and Tcf21-KO at 16 weeks? From figure 4A, the overall change seems negligible when compared to the decrease in FMC1 and CMC. Is the overall increase in atherosclerosis in Tcf21-KO attributed mainly to the expansion of SMC3, given the lack of changes FMC2 population? Another mechanism that might play a role beside the changes in phenotypic switching or percentages of modulated SMC population in Tcf21-KO is their localization. Is there a significant change in the localization of FMC2, FMC1, CMC and particularly SMC3 population in control vs Tcf21 KO?
Minor Points
• Does the osteoblast, senescence, EMT, apoptosis, angiogenesis or efferocytosis cell state of SMC3 changes between control and Tcf21?
• Can the authors provide the actual percentages of the 6 different SMC subpopulations at all timepoints in Fig 2C?
• Given that control TCF21 + IgG showed some unspecific background PLA signal, it would be worth it to show the second control (TEAD1 + IgG) and quantifications of the background signal in the negative controls as well as in TCF21 + TEAD1. It seems that there is also significant interaction between Tcf21p and Tead1p in the cytosol as well. Given this, it would be better to include more information regarding the images. Are they epifluorescence or laser confocal images? If epifluorescence, are they deconvolved and how? Are they max projection or single slices (mentioning objective + NA and pinhole size, or optical slide depth)?
• PLA assays detects proximity of proteins up to max of 35~ 40 nm, well above the Rmin of the predicted dimer for TcF21-Tead1 interaction, thus it is still not direct proof of binding/interaction between these protein. Can/did the authors try coIP? (acknowledging coIP from nuclear lysates can be difficult). This would provide better evidence of physical interaction between these two protein or coIP their intermediate if the interaction is not direct.
• It seems that other TF besides the KLF family and AP1 factors, such as Smad2 and Smad3, also show a bimodal open motif distribution. Could they be playing a dual role in early SMC to FMC transition as well?
• Figure 4B: label the top Sankey plot as “Control” and bottom as “Tcf21-KO” in the graph, not only mentioning it in the figure legend
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This is a detailed and comprehensive single-cell and epigenomic study on VSMC transitions in atherosclerosis in the context of CAD. It aimed to study trajectories of SMC state transitions, identify novel TFs and gene regulatory networks contributing to these transitions, and how the Tcf21 gene regulates these processes. Key findings included the identification of six SMC states, with the FMC-1 and FMC-2 states contributing to CMC. Tcf21 emerged as the top regulator for the SMC to FMC transition, along with other TFs, ie. Runx, Klf4, Smad3, HIF etc. Tcf21 KO resulted in reduced FMC and CMCs and increased SMCs, and TEAD1 was found to interact with Tcf21 to modulate TGFB and ECM-related profibrotic pathways.
Strengths:
The authors utilized advanced multi-omic tools such as single-cell multi-omics (scRNA+scATAC) and technical computational modeling (ie. WOT, CellOracle, Pando..etc). They conducted lineage traced atherosclerosis mouse model experiments to assess the transition of SMC switching across 4 time points and the role of Tcf21. They assessed translational relevance by integrating with human genetic data (GWAS, scDRS, S-PrediXcan). They discovered a novel mechanism in the Tcf21-TEAD1 interaction and importantly identified FMC2 as a key CAD-risk state.
Weaknesses:
1. Three key findings were that 1) Tcf21 plays a strong role as a driver of contractile SMCs transitioning to FMC-1 and that 2) FMC-2 was identified as the key FMC cluster associated with CAD risk. 3) Knocking out Tcf21 led to decreased FMC1 and FMC2 and CMC proportions and increased SMC2 and SMC3 at 12 weeks, and further decrease of FMC1 but not FMC2 at 16 weeks. Since this was the case, did the authors consider another major candidate regulator/TF associated with driving SMCs to FMC2 (ie. TEAD1?) since this seems to be a very important natural point to the study’s narrative?
2. The authors provide important in situ transcript validation using RNAScope. However, additional protein-level validation of FMC markers would strengthen the evidence beyond the RNA landscape towards functional cell phenotypes.
3. The evidence of the role of TEAD1 from ChIP-seq and reporter assays support TEAD1 as a TCF21 partner. Functional perturbation of TEAD1 would significantly strengthen the mechanistic conclusions.
4. If the conclusion is that Tcf21 promotes the protective FMC1 and competes with TEAD1 which promotes the CAD-risk-enriched state FMC2, it may be be important to know whether TEAD1 acts as an independent disease promoting factor or modulates risk through its interaction with TCF21.
5. The use of CellOracle provided a rich set of candidate TFs for driving SMC phenotypic switching. With the exception of Tcf21, some (even limited) validation of additional TFs could strengthen conclusions made.
6. Some functional validation in primary SMCs to identify and distinguish FMC1 and FMC2 would strengthen the story inferred from the multi-omics data.
Minor corrections:
Figure 6 legend: repeat of “and” in title.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewer Comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author)
In the paper “Vascular smooth muscle cell state trajectories mediate molecular mechanisms of coronary disease risk”, Li, Kundu et al. studied smooth muscle cell state transition measured by transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility in mouse aortic root across ApoE-/- induced atherosclerosis dense time points. The authors linked fibroblast and osteochondrogenic phenotype in smooth muscle cells to atherosclerotic states in transcriptomics and in special organization. The fibroblast-like cells (fibromyocytes, FMCs) had two subtypes, one of which was associated with immune activation and the other was associated with fibrous cap spanning the intimal plaque. The osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (chondrocytes, CMCs) had a distinct chromatin accessibility pattern. The authors further performed Waddington optimal transport to explore cell state transitions. There was an increase in FMC and CMC states at the atherosclerosis endpoint. The authors identified transcription factors enriched across cell state transitions. With aligned scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data, the authors identified cell state specific transcription factor motifs from scATAC-seq data across pseudotime points. Gene regulatory network analysis in the co-embedded scRNA and scATAC dataset showed Tcf21 enrichment in SMC-FMC transition. The authors further performed knockout on Tcf21 and observed increase in SMC-3 cluster in early time points and decrease in FCM and CMC cell states at late atherosclerosis states. TCF21 was also found to interact with TEAD1 gene in vitro. An integrated analysis showed that FMC and CMC cell states have higher enrichment of CAD GWAS genes. Overall, the authors conducted a carefully designed time course experiment to identify critical cell state transitions, the underlying cellular process, and key genes that drive atherosclerosis in smooth muscle cells. The analysis is novel, and the underlying data will be a wonderful resource for the vascular biology field.
Question/Suggestions:
1. Was there heterogeneity in TdTomato expression in the cells analyzed? Would be good to show a feature plot for TdTomato expression to determine if there were cell-types that started with less expression of Myh11.
Thank you, this is an important question. We show in Supp Fig 1 that there is a bimodal distribution of tdTomato expression which likely represents ambient RNA or doublets which incorporated tdTomato expressing cells (as discussed in Sharma et al.1). To address your question more directly, we have now included an additional panel (Supp Fig 1H) to show the distribution of tdTomato at baseline to demonstrate the specificity of Myh11 driven tdTomato distribution. It is important to remember that recombination efficiency is quite high, ~95%, so cells expressing even low levels of Myh11 will activate the high-level expression of the tdTomato reporter, which does not really reflect endogenous Myh11 expression level.
Results, line 119:
All of the phenotype clusters represented cells of the SMC lineage, as indicated by lineage tracing with the Myh11-Cre transgene (Fig. 1H). It is important to note that recombination efficiency is quite high, ~95%, so cells expressing even low levels of Myh11 will activate the high-level expression of the tdTomato reporter, which does not really reflect endogenous Myh11 expression level that might reflect some heterogeneity in the SMC cell population.
2. The main figures have been rasterized, so many figures are unreadable. Figure 1 O-Q, for example, are completely unreadable.
Thank you for pointing this out. We apologize for this mistake and have re-rendered all of the images to fit the quality standards for the submission.
3. Discussion section would benefit from comparison between Waddington OT and other trajectory analysis methods? For example, CellRank is widely used, and would be helpful to know the nuances that motivated the use of Waddington OT.
At the time of our data development and temporal analyses, Waddington OT was a well-utilized trajectory method that incorporated experimental time as a key feature in addition to modeling of variable cell growth rate/death (cell cycle and apoptosis) signatures derived from transcriptomic profiles rather than just comparing cell-cell expression similarity. We further selected time points based on clear real time phenotypic stages that occur in the data, which is another key assumption in this method. This allowed for a unified framework for further time-course based analyses.
Similar real-time based methods such as those incorporated in CellRank22 had been just described in preprint and so we again, decided to apply well-utilized orthogonal methods from the original CellRank3, such as its pseudotime kernel, to generate a probabilistic model, which appears to follow similar patterns as our optimal transport approach. This provided the added advantage of placing critical TFs across time in a sequential pattern to follow the cascade of transcription factor activation.
Taken together, these methods expand upon initial studies which only used pseudotime to infer disease trajectories in this murine atherosclerosis model4,5. We have now incorporated these points into the discussion section with the following text.
Discussion, line 600:
Computational algorithms used in these studies were identified to be those most aligned and broadly tested with the genomic and genetic data types provided in our timecourse study. In particular, novel trajectory methods that become available may continue to offer useful and more nuanced details regarding the complex cell state changes that the SMC undergo during the disease process and we make our data available for such analyses. While the WOT approach was specifically designed for timecourse scRNAseq data, the CellRank22 algorithm is now considered to potentially yield more accurate and robust results by integrating additional biological information, such as metabolic labeling, and can use optimal transport as one component of its broader multivariate analysis. We did in fact utilize orthogonal methods from the original CellRank3, such as its pseudotime kernel, to generate a probabilistic model, which appeared to follow similar patterns as our WOT approach to generate interpretable summary models.
4. Current in situ hybridization is only show at 1 time point (Figure 1L,M,N). If this can be done at a few time points it would validate there is a migratory path.
We agree that this is an important point and performed additional RNAScope to follow-up on this recommendation. We performed RNAScope at baseline and 7 weeks of high fat diet (HFD) to resolve the localization of top FMC-1 and FMC-2 markers (Fbln1, Fbln2, respectively) to show that at baseline, Fbln1 is seen at low level in the media and Fbln2 is not. Then, at 7 weeks of HFD, there is enrichment of Fbln1 in the media and at the cap (at lower levels) while Fbln2 is more restricted to the intima when compared with FMC-1. It is important to note that the comparisons of Fbln1 and 2 in these slides represent serial sections, therefore, highlighting the beginning differences in expression pattern between these marker genes. This aligns closely with our single cell data which shows low level FMC-1 but no FMC-2 marker expression at baseline while FMC-1 and FMC-2 expression ramps up by week 7 of HFD. These results are shown in the revised manuscript (Fig. 2B, C, S-Fig. 3N, O).
Further, we expanded our cell transition localization analysis with high quality Xenium 5k geneset data for the mouse aorta and its branches. With transfer of single cell RNA sequencing labels to the spatial clusters, we demonstrated that FMC-1 signals are enriched in the media and also sporadically localized in the cap by 16 weeks of HFD. Subsequently high levels of FMC-2 were identified in the cap and spanning the intima to the CMCs at the base of the plaque, further validating our inference based on selected RNAScope markers. The additional Xenium data are provided (Fig. 1P, Q, S, S-Fig. 2A) and related text is provided in the Results section of the manuscript.
Results, line 167:
To examine the translocation of FMC from media to cap to plaque, we performed additional studies to map temporal gene expression of FMC-1 and FMC-2 marker genes Fbln1 and Fbln2 across serial sections to highlight their distinct expression patterns. RNAScope performed at baseline showed that FMC-1 marker Fbln1 expression was seen in the media while expression of FMC-2 maker Fbln2 was not (S-Fig. 3N). Then, at 7 weeks of high fat diet (HFD), there was enrichment of Fbln1 in the media and at lower levels at the cap, while Fbln2 was more intimally restricted with lower medial expression compared with FMC-1. (S-Fig. 3N, O). These findings aligned with our single cell data which showed low level FMC-1 but no FMC-2 marker expression at baseline while FMC-1 and FMC-2 expression increased after week 7 of HFD (Fig. 2A, B, C). We further investigated the lesion cellular anatomy at 16 weeks HFD with high quality Xenium 5k geneset data for the mouse aorta. With transfer of single cell RNA sequencing labels to the spatial clusters, we demonstrated that FMC-1 are enriched in the media and also localized in the cap after 16 weeks HFD. Subsequently high levels of FMC-2 were identified in the cap and spanning the intima to the CMCs at the base of the plaque, further validating our inference based on selected RNAScope markers (Fig. 1O-T, S-Fig. 2A).
For our spatial analysis, we have incorporated the new methods in the Materials and Methods section of the manuscript.
Materials and Methods, line 811:
Xenium Slide Processing and analysis
Fresh frozen tissue sections were prepared following the 10x Genomics Xenium In Situ for Fresh Frozen Tissues Protocol (CG000579 Rev F). Briefly, tissues arranged in order of aortic root, ascending aorta, brachiocephalic artery with right subclavian branch, per-diaphragmatic descending, and abdominal descending aorta from a control (TgMyh11-CreERT2, Tcf21+/+, ROSAtdT/+, ApoE−/−) mouse were embedded in OCT compound immediately after dissection. Embedded tissue blocks were frozen on dry ice and immediately stored at -80C prior to sectioning.
Sections of 10m thickness were cut using a Leica CM1860 cryostat. Sections were mounted within the sample area (10.45 x 22.45mm) of Xenium slides (PN-3000941) without overlap and stored at -80C until ready for use. All subsequent Xenium steps were processed at the Stanford Functional Genomics Core. Tissue morphology and quality was assessed using Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) and DAPI staining prior to downstream Xenium In Situ Gene Expression assays.
Processed Xenium datasets were imported into Seurat V5 for normalization and integration. Feature-barcode matrices were normalized using the SCTransform workflow with spatial coordinates retained for downstream deconvolution. To perform single-cell reference label transfer to the Xenium data, canonical correlation analysis (CCA) was implemented following strategies from the Seurat tutorial “Analysis, visualization, and integration of spatial datasets with Seurat” (https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/spatial_vignette.html). RCTD (Robust Cell Type Decomposition) was applied to further deconvolve spot-level spatial data based on input cell reference.
Minor comments:
5. Is there spatial specific expression quantification for Fig 1L,M,N?
Given the specificity of the cellular localization and the low background with the RNAscope hybridization, and the strong correlation with the single cell data we did not feel that quantitation of the RNAscope was necessary. We have since also added Xenium data to further validate our observations with selected RNAScope markers and also as a public resource for future studies. We feel that quantitation of cell numbers for the different transition phenotypes is best reflected by the cluster cell numbers in the scRNAseq data.
6. The authors listed several transcription factors found through WOT analysis and TF enrichment in the paragraph from line 173 to 191. It will be good to have a summary describing how FMC and CMC regulate proliferation during atherosclerosis.
We thank the Reviewer for this suggestion. We have now included an additional supplementary table (S-Table 7 ) to describe the function of TFs related to optimal transport/cell oracle nominated TFs, including regarding proliferation and other cell state changes.
Results, line 204:
Across the enriched TFs found in our model, several patterns stand out. For example, TFs (Runx1/2, Zbtb7c, Zeb1/2, Smad3, Stat3, Hes1, Nfkb1, Cebpb) amongst this list have been readily associated in literature with AP-1, Klfs and the SMC regulatory Srf-myocardin complex. This suggests that pioneer factors and immediate-early AP-1 activation constitute a core early event that then allows for recruitment of transcription factors at specific enhancers to drive key cell state transition steps in conjunction with Srf-myocardin. These core TFs then organize around central cellular processes such as TGFB signaling, hypoxia signaling, inflammatory response and osteochondrogenesis as summarized in S-Table 76-10.
7. How were the PseudoEarly and PseudoLate bins determined in scATAC-seq analysis? Since there is scATAC-seq data taken at each time point, could the authors perform enrichment analysis based on the cell state clusters within each time point? Would a random separation of pseudotime points show similar TF enrichment results? The random separation TF enrichment analysis could potentially show significance of the selected SMC-FMC and FMC-CMC transitions.
Thank you for this comment. The PseudoEarly and PseudoLate bins are based on the distribution of cell state clusters where the majority of phenotypically transitioning cluster cells are covered by the PseudoLate bins (bins 25-30). This was demonstrated by the distribution of cell clusters in Figure 3A. However, this was shown only by a small graphic above the heatmap, and we now have highlighted the timepoint and cluster designations with expanded bar graphs above the ATAC pathway clustering in Figure 3A. Further, we have made additional clarifications in the text and figure legends to highlight the importance of these expanded graphics Although there are multiple timepoints for the scATAC data, because all clusters are represented in the later timepoints, TF enrichment analyses on a timepoint basis may not accurately delineate transitioning TF motif enrichment. Therefore, we took a pseudotime approach, which not only showed a strong correlation with the appearance of cell state clusters over time, but also helped unify our analysis across all the timepoints.
We further investigated the question regarding random separation of pseudotime bins to assess how TF enrichment may shift. We utilized the pseudotime aggregated ChromVar scores and randomly shuffled the 30 pseudotime bins 1000 times by bootstrapping and created an average pseudotime bin distribution. Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, the authors continue their longstanding strong work of using advanced multiome computational genomic tools with mouse and human genetics to elucidate the cell fate of SMC and their contribution to atherosclerosis progression. Here, the authors present a comprehensive single cell transcriptomic and epigenomic analysis of SMC populations and apply probabilistic Waddington Optimal transport (WOT) modeling across a timecourse of atherosclerosis progression (in a mouse ApoE KO model) to define dynamic SMC cell states and trajectories. By integrating scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq over time, with many more timepoints than most studies, they are able to infer a higher resolution TF regulon network to predict the top drivers of SMC phenotypic switching (SMC types, n=3) to fibromyocyte (FMC types, n=2) and to chondromyocytes (CMC). Furthermore, they use their previous model, Tcf21 KO, to gain further insight as to the changes in SMC transdifferentiation in this current work and to validate their in-silico TF perturbation computational predictions. Importantly, they integrated human CAD GWAS studies to associate changes in SMC subpopulations and cell states with disease risk in humans. Overall, in comparison to their previous work in Sharma, et al, ATVB, 2024, they now present a deeper genomic, transcriptional, and regulatory view rather than descriptive model of SMC phenotypic switching linked to human disease. This new work is technically rigorous and leverages multiome single cell sequencing data with advanced computational analysis to provide new regulatory insights into the relationship between SMC phenotypic switching and CAD.
We thank the Reviewer for these laudatory comments.
Major Points:
• The detailed time course, computational rigor and the use of Tcf21 KO data (an established CAD gene already well studied by this group) to probe the models are strengths. Yet the reliance alone on Tcf21 as the genetic probe has limitations and reduces the novelty given how much work this group has already done on Tcf21 KO mouse models and Tcf21 human genetics. And, despite the deep dive with multiple time points and integrated computational multi-omics approaches, the inferences are confusing in places.
Based on human genetics and mouse genetic models prior work infers that TCF21 may serve a protective role in atherosclerosis. This serves as a grounding for interpretation of cell states, trajectories and their regulation and their function in disease. Yet, Tcf21 is found to regulate (increase) FMC cell state – inferred as protective - and also regulate (increase) CMCs - proposed to be harmful. Based on human genetics, the authors interpret the important disease related cell regulation as FMC increase and the inferred Tcf21-mediated CMC increase to be a downstream mass effect that is not important (not harmful) but there is no direct data to support that conclusion.
We believe that these studies have provided considerable novel information regarding the specific role of TCF21 toward regulation of SMC phenotype transitions and disease risk. The Reviewer is correct that TCF21 is now a highly validated CAD GWAS causal gene and represents an archetypal contributor to SMC phenotypic transitions that by inference from human genetics represent a protective mechanism toward disease risk. However, our original single cell RNA sequencing studies published in Wirka et al.13 employed early (v2) 10x chemistry and thus provided a limited characterization of the cellular and molecular effects of Tcf21 in the disease setting, and was not paired with single cell epigenetic profiling. Importantly, we did not have sufficient cells and identified genes in that study to fully characterize the chondromyocyte (CMC) phenotype. We thus included Tcf21 knockout in these comprehensive temporal transcriptomic and epigenomic studies to place it in the SMC transitional regulatory framework, and link TCF21 to other CAD associated factors that promote or inhibit risk in this context. Through these studies we have shown that Tcf21 inhibits transition of secondary heart field cells to a differentiated SMC phenotype we have labeled SMC-3, placed Tcf21 function in the FMC1 subpopulation of the fibromyocyte cell phenotype, and characterized the disease regulon of Tcf21 target genes. These findings have significantly expanded our understanding of its cellular and molecular functions, but as discussed below, also identified some confusing features regarding its role in the transition from FMC to CMC transition phenotype.
The comments by the Reviewer have also prompted us to reconsider our previous studies, and to incorporate the Klf4 KO analyses into our considerations regarding SMC disease causality and the FMC2 and CMC transition phenotypes. Previous studies in our initially suggested that transition to the CMC phenotype might be the mechanism of disease risk for SMC lineage cells. Mouse knockout studies for the CAD protective orthologous human SMAD3 gene revealed increased CMC transition, vascular calcification, and disease burden4. Knockout of the CAD disease promoting PDGFD mouse ortholog revealed decreased CMC numbers and decreased vascular calcification, and while there was no change in plaque burden there were a number of other cellular features consistent with plaque destabilization, including increased inflammatory profile and macrophage recruitment. Knockout of the mouse Ahr gene further substantiated the correlation of CMC transition phenotype to vascular calcification and disease burden. These findings, in conjunction with extensive clinical and epidemiology data suggesting that vascular calcification is a strong predictor of CAD risk, and likely causal contributor to disease pathology14-16, our initial hypothesis was that the CMC phenotype and related vascular calcification is the mechanism by which CAD associated primarily SMC lineage genes promote disease risk. It was unclear at that time whether FMC represented a transition phenotype or possibly a stable phenotype that might have a protective effect, possibly retarding transition to the disease promoting CMC transition. Thus our expectation going into these studies was that knockout of the protective Tcf21 gene would lead to an increase in CMC and that this cellular phenotype would show evidence of increased risk.
In an effort to assign genetic disease risk to SMC state transitions we conducted studies reported here employing single cell disease relevance score (scDRS) analyses to gain insights linking SMC transition phenotype and genetic disease risk and these analyses pointed to the FMC-2 phenotype. It was a surprising but also important finding that these methods did not assign genetic risk to the CMC, but this observation in conjunction with the strong evidence that protective gene Tcf21 promotes transition to the CMC phenotype led us to propose a unifying model that genetic risk predominantly resides in the FMC-2 phenotype, and not the CMC phenotype, with the corollary that Tcf21 promotes an increase in non-disease promoting CMC through a simple “mass action” effect.
These Reviewer comments have led us to re-examine these data and to try and better integrate the directionality from genetic risk assessment with disease lesion features and risk prediction as linked to single cell gene expression and phenotype.
As noted by the reviewer we do not have evidence that convincingly eliminates the possibility that CMC contribute CAD risk, and this observation has led us to examine the correlation between SMC phenotype and the contribution of the extensively validated gene Klf4 to disease risk. To accomplish this, we did label transfer of our atherosclerosis time-course trajectory to the Klf4-KO data17, and found that knockout of this gene produced a prominent decrease in CMC number (20% vs 52%) that correlated with the previously described decrease in disease burden, fibrous cap contribution, and the identified osteochondrogenic cluster 7 transcriptional phenotype. These data in conjunction with our previous correlation of disease features with causal gene functions for Smad3, Pdgfd and Ahr has provided a compelling case for us to re-consider our model, focusing on the statistical and bioinformatic analyses that are in line with disease lesion features, and suggests a role for the CMC phenotype toward clinical disease risk.
We consider our finding of FMC-2 disease causality to be robust, and the analysis is supported by work published by Ord et al.5 using linkage disequilibrium analysis to show cells expressing Vcam1, essentially FMC-1 and FMC-2 combined, are the primary contributors to disease risk for the SMC lineage. Further, our scDRS analysis of data from Pan et al.18 also finds similar FMC-2 enriched genetic risk (S-Fig. 4A-C). Importantly, there are a number of reasons why CMC might not show risk with the scDRS algorithm. An important point is that there are actually few osteochondrogenic genes that reside in CAD risk loci, and this is surprising given the extensive list of chondrogenic development genes that are expressed in these cells. Perhaps allelic variation arising in these loci is lost through purifying selection. Interestingly, we did find greater differences in gene expression for the individual CMC genes that were included in the scDRS analysis, but the number of genes was not sufficient to provide a statistical association. For these reasons, we now take a broader view of the relationship of SMC transitions to disease risk, with both the FMC-2 and CMC considered as likely contributors to risk.
Combining all available data, we now propose the hypothesis that FMC-2 provide a primarily protective role while CMC likely function to promote vascular calcification and disease risk.
Thus in the revised manuscript we continue to support the risk analyses that identify causal evidence for a risk-determining protective effect of FMC-2 phenotype cells. New to the revised manuscript, we propose a heuristic model that assigns CAD risk to the pro-calcification CMC phenotype cells, based on correlation of this cell state with disease burden and direction of human genetic risk. We point to a need for future research that identifies a greater number of CAD causal genes, especially those that are in keeping with the osteochondrogenic CMC molecular processes, that will allow more sophisticated assessment of risk ascertainment as focused on the transition to this SMC lineage phenotype. Further, we no longer present the mass action hypothesis to explain the TCF21 generation of CMC that do not contribute to disease risk but highlight the need to study the functional role of the CMC phenotype in general, and especially Tcf21-KO lineage CMC, i.e., how they may differ from non-Tcf21-KO lineage CMC in the context of disease risk. These points are now articulated in the Discussion with the following text:
Discussion, line 570:
We and others have used CAD GWAS findings along with gene expression or chromatin accessibility data to show that much of the risk for CAD resides in the coronary vascular SMC lineage5,19-21. Our high-resolution dataset extends upon previous observations and identifies FMC-2 as the cell state harboring significant CAD risk, based on disease gene expression integration with scDRS and PrediXcan, and suggests that the FMC-2 cell state is a protective mechanism toward human CAD risk (Fig. 6A). In situ RNA staining localizes the FMC-2 population to both the fibrous cap (Notch3, Thbs1) and the intimal plaque (Fbln2, Ttc9) confirmed with label transfer using Xenium spatial transcriptomics. Further molecular analysis finds FMC-2 at the juncture of critical gene modules for senescence and apoptosis while expressing numerous CAD associated genes that we have linked to atherosclerosis, including ZEB2 and SMAD34,22.Using this scDRS score leverages the power of GWAS genes to identify likely causal cell state determining genes whose functions are critical to prime cells towards phenotypic transition.
The scDRS analysis did not identify CAD risk in the CMC phenotype cells. This is surprising, given that mouse knockout disease models of orthologs of human CAD associated genes SMAD3 and PDGFD4,23, and other genes not yet linked to CAD by GWAS, KLF4 and AHR17,24, have demonstrated a significant correlation between CMC number, plaque burden, and vascular calcification. This is true for both disease promoting and disease protective gene functions, as determined by effect allele identification and genetics of gene expression data. It is possible that there is a dearth of informative allelic variation in CAD loci that determine the CMC phenotype. We did observe that aggregate expression of CAD disease risk genes in the CMC cell state showed a higher relative average expression of CAD GWAS risk genes, but this did not provide a statistically significant result. This observation suggests that a bias against regulatory variation at the CMC determining gene loci resulting in a low number of informative genes may explain the lack of an scDRS finding. Also, an important consideration is that FMC2 are the most similar to CMC in terms of gene expression phenotype, and the risk identified in these cells may not be protective but may in fact promote disease risk through directing differentiation to the CMC phenotype. eQTL based directionality inference is limited by the number of genes that have statistically significant eQTL links and this can bias results. Finally, the observation that Tcf21 promotes transition to the CMC phenotype is difficult to reconcile with these considerations but may simply reflect that the protective effect of increased FMC number outweighs the disease promoting effect of increased CMC.
Discussion, line 626:
Future studies are needed to confirm the functions of nominated novel genes implicated in the cell state changes characterized through these studies. Only through study of the larger causal gene regulatory network will we be able to understand which aspects of the complex cellular phenotypic changes, migratory behaviors and cell-cell interactions that are responsible for the risk that is modulated by the SMC lineage. Specifically, studies are needed to characterize in greater detail the FMC-2 phenotype genes that regulate CAD risk, what is the nature of CMC disease risk, and how can disease protective genes like TCF21 promote CMC formation without increasing risk.
The required expansive causal CAD gene characterization can only come from large-scale in vitro CRISPR screening with highly relevant disease cellular models, and similar screens conducted in disease model mice which will provide in vivo disease transcriptomic phenotype information regarding the function of SMC genes that both regulate SMC phenotype and CAD risk.
Similarly, the authors provide evidence that FMC1 and FMC2 can be terminal cell states but that some FMCs can transition to more harmful CMC… yet it is completely unclear what might regulate the transition or lack of transition of FMC types to CMCs – which appears to be an important cellular functional event in disease. The authors should be more circumspect in their interpretation and interrogate more comprehensively these contradictions in their data. Ideally, they would interrogate separate data (even if limited and public) for an independent and opposing key regulator of SMC phenotype switching e.g., Klf4.
We agree with the Reviewer that it is critical to identify genes that promote and inhibit the SMC-FMC and FMC-CMC transitions, and the current study was performed to further address this specific need. With work reported in this manuscript we have taken the first step, to identify and characterize in detail the cellular transition phenotypes and the genes and regulons that are predicted to regulate the critical cell state changes. Perhaps most important is the gene regulatory network that is functional in the FMC2 population of cells, which are the closest in phenotype to the CMC and likely are the “master regulators” of whether these cells transition to disease risk CMC or remain in a protective FMC2 phenotype. We have already shown that CAD protective gene Zeb2 promotes transition to the FMC phenotype, and possibly more importantly disrupts transition to the CMC phenotype22. Other genes that are identified with WOT analyses described in this manuscript, in addition to TCF21, include Ahr, Runx2, and Sox9, Gas7 and an inflammatory module that includes Irf5 and Nfkb, all of which are also likely regulators of the FMC2-CMC transition. Further studies are needed to assess these factors as modulators of the FMC2-CMC transition. We have now established methodology for in vivo Perturb-seq studies and will be able to investigate changes in transcriptional phenotype of SMC lineage cells in the disease setting with CRISPRi mediated gene knockdown and individual cell whole genome scRNAseq. These studies should allow us to identify which of these genes promote the FMC-CMC transition.
Also, as noted above we integrated scRNAseq data from the Owens lab characterizing the cellular and molecular features associated with Klf4 expression in the SMC lineage in the disease setting. Comparison of wildtype and Klf4 KO clusters showed a significant decrease in FMC-2 and CMC cell numbers with Klf4 deletion. This group of cells corresponds with the author’s Phactr1 staining which showed SMC media and fibrous cap enrichment, where we have localized this cell phenotype. Also, these findings are in line with our CellOracle predictions (Fig 3I) where Klf4 was predicted to be a lead gene promoting FMC to CMC transition. They also demonstrate the importance of the FMC2 population whereby decreased cells of this phenotype then results in decreased CMC, especially in the context of Klf4 knockout.
With respect to some subset of FMC1 and FMC2 populations being terminally differentiated based on data at 16 weeks of western diet (WD), more temporal data should be added especially as 16 weeks WD may not capture the complexity of later lesions and human disease. It is important to include a longer timepoint on WD, ~ 20 or 26 weeks, to determine if this holds true. Furthermore, this would also better elucidate the trajectory of CMC population with atherosclerosis progression and more advanced disease.

Our comprehensive multi-omic dataset has enabled the profiling of TF motif accessibility gradients across time and leveraged these data to generate regulatory networks, prioritize key driver genes and evaluate their functional pathways. Materials and Methods, Line 842:
Processing of external datasets Pan et al., Alencar et al., Cheng et al.
Data from Pan et al. (GSE155513)18, Alencar et al (GSE150644)17, Cheng et al. (PRJNA794806)4 were downloaded and reprocessed using standard 10x CellRanger pipeline as noted above to facilitate label transfer analysis with our timecourse dataset. All subsetting parameters and clustering parameters decisions were made based on available published methods, following prior settings as closely as possible. For the Pan et al. dataset, we performed further data pruning, subsetting based on fluorescent marker expression as previously described in Sharma et al.1. We then applied cutoffs of nFeature > 1900, percent.mt < 7.5 to match our control timecourse study. For clustering, we identified top 1500 variable genes and generated UMAP with 20 principal components (PCs) as previously described. For Alencar et al. we filtered on nFeature_RNA > 200 and < 5000, percent.mt < 10. 19 PCs were selected for clustering. The clustering resolution was not specified. This does not affect our downstream analysis, as the goal for this analysis is to understand the distribution of label-transfer clusters from our control timecourse study. For Cheng et al. we requested original processed script from the author to recreate the R-Smad clustering. After clustering of these datasets, we then performed CCA label transfer followed by generation of confusion matrices to compare and contrast the relationship between clusters and identify existing cell states.
The authors use WOT algorithm that was initially developed by Eric Lander’s and Aviv Regev’s labs to improve upon already available methods for cell trajectory or lineage inferring across developing tissues. However, all these methods, including the one in this manuscript, lacks the cellular resolution to accurately infer lineage tracing, specially for rarer populations. This seems evident by the apparent lack of origin of FMC2 subcluster at the earlier timepoints (~ 5 Wk). While the Sankey representation of inferred transition of state in Fig 3D clearly shows the transition SMC2 -> FMC1 -> FMC2 or SMC2 -> FMC2 in the later timepoints, it seems to have a problem inferring transition state changes for FMC2 at 5 wk. A similar issue is encountered with CMC population in the Tcf21 KO at 12 and 16 wks. The authors must comment about the temporal and cellular resolution limits of this approach and strategies to possibly improve it (i.e. adding timepoints in between?).
We initially attempted to create a unifying transition probability figure for 2C and 3D that that not only showed representative cell proportions at each timepoint but also the transition probability with size of transition bands relative to the starting band width at each time point. Unfortunately, due to problems with rasterization of the figure images, the lines in the Sankey plots connecting FMC-1 to FMC-2 at the 5-week time-point may not be readily visualized. This is due to a small, but present, population of FMC-1 at baseline, reducing the probability of transition of FMC-1 to FMC-2. With this caveat in mind, we have recreated the visualization to just show relative proportion of change in Fig. 2D and emphasize in the text that the actual proportion of each cell state at each time point can be observed in Fig. 2C. With our current visualization, we try to balance relative proportional changes as well as the initial proportion of each cluster. We did not pursue this visualization initially, because we did not want to create the false sense that cell proportions are equal at each timepoint but unfortunately clearly introduced other unintended confusion with this plot. These new plots have now replaced the initial Fig 2C and 3D within the Results section of the manuscript. With this change, the relative proportion changes are more apparent for the FMC1-FMC2 transition in 2D with ~20% probability and FMC-CMC probability in 3C with low probability from both FMC-1 and FMC-2.
Overall, as the reviewer correctly pointed out, this reflects the important observation that current methods may lack the fidelity to infer transition for more rare populations, which is why we utilized more conservative cutoffs throughout our study to develop a reproducible trajectory model for SMC transitions. Furthermore, this highlights the limitation of available methods where adequate representation of cell states, is necessary due to the inability to perform accurate zero-shot inference while simply adding additional datapoints also makes trajectory inference more difficult due to incremental changes in cellular proportion. Our strategy with available methods straddles the middle ground where we generate multiple timepoints to confirm trends in cellular proportion change and carefully select representative timepoints that show appropriate cell state proportion change to facilitate trajectory analysis.

We compared the module scores in SMC-3 between Tcf21-KO and control using Wilcoxon rank sum test and made the following observations using a Bonferroni corrected p=0.008 as the significance cutoff threshold (for 6 comparisons in SMC-3). Co-Immunoprecipitation

This is a detailed and comprehensive single-cell and epigenomic study on VSMC transitions in atherosclerosis in the context of CAD. 1. Three key findings were that 1) Tcf21 plays a strong role as a driver of contractile SMCs transitioning to FMC-1 and that 2) FMC-2 was identified as the key FMC cluster associated with CAD risk. 3) Knocking out Tcf21 led to decreased FMC1 and FMC2 and CMC proportions and increased SMC2 and SMC3 at 12 weeks, and further decrease of FMC1 but not FMC2 at 16 weeks. TEAD1?) since this seems to be a very important natural point to the study’s narrative?

Based on our findings, we interpret the cell state changes from Tcf21 knockout as a direct effect on FMC-1 and an indirect effect on FMC-2 with compensation by week 16. Given our prediction from fate correlation analysis that Tcf21 acts upstream of Zeb2, and experimental evidence confirming that TCF21 binds and regulates ZEB2 expression, we re-analyzed our prior Zeb2 mouse atherosclerosis knockout data22. We performed label transfer and found that there was also a significant decrease in FMC-1 but not FMC-2. We interrogated differentially expressed genes with DESeq2 and identified increases in Tead1 as well as co-activator Yap1 within the FMC-2 cluster, suggesting that these factors are compensating for Tcf21 loss and maintaining FMC-2 cell numbers.
In addition, we also further interrogated our control mice gene regulatory networks and were intrigued to identify Tead1 as a downstream target of Zeb2, and Mecom – the two top transcription factors that are predicted to be Tcf21 targets. Both Zeb2 and Mecom were predicted to suppress Tead1 expression in this context which is validated with Tead1 increase in the Zeb2 knockout study.
Moreover, our repeat analysis of the Klf4 KO data has shown that this factor, which promotes FMC-CMC transition, regulates Tead1 expression. Other transcription factors predicted to be involved with Tead1 include AP-1 factors such as Fos and Atf3, which are core TFs that have a role in regulating smooth muscle identity.
As outlined below, we have performed extensive in vitro studies to link Tead1 and the Yap pathway with Tcf21 interactions in the context of SMC transitions, DNA binding and transcription, and collaboration with Tcf21 to regulate disease risk mechanisms. We fully agree with the Reviewer’s hypothesis regarding the SMC transition role for Tead1, however, to extend our understanding of Tead1 in greater detail will require more extensive studies with a direct focus on this factor, employing a cell-specific model and extensive study of TEAD1 contribution to CAD risk, and we feel that these studies are beyond the scope of the current work.
2. The authors provide important in situ transcript validation using RNAScope. However, additional protein-level validation of FMC markers would strengthen the evidence beyond the RNA landscape towards functional cell phenotypes.

While we agree that protein-level confirmation would be valuable, we felt that in our hands individual antibody studies are extremely time-consuming and difficult to scale at this point. We are looking at spatial proteomics as a method that will provide the type of data that will be truly transformative for studies such as those noted by the reviewer, and we hope to implement this work in the coming months. Other protein-based imaging (e.g., high throughput immunofluorescence or imaging mass cytometry) will also further strengthen the single cell transcriptomic findings as high‑quality reagents can be identified.
However, to provide robust, orthogonal validation that preserves spatial context, we performed in situ spatial transcriptomics using the Xenium 5k panel, a state‑of‑the‑art platform that quantifies thousands of transcripts with single‑cell/subcellular resolution across multiple segments of the mouse aorta to further validate our nominated cell states (Fig. 1P-T, S-Fig. 2A). To the best of our knowledge, this will be the first such single cell resolution dataset to be generated for mouse aortic atherosclerosis and will significantly aid the research of groups in the field. As another tool that expands the utility of single cell transcriptomics, we leveraged label transfer from our time-course to assign cell‑state identities using the robust cell type decomposition (RCTD) algorithm. These analyses demonstrate strong concordance between the cell states nominated in our discovery data and those observed in situ, further validating the anatomic niches and co-localization patterns described in our study.

We performed TEAD1 knockdown with siRNA and evaluated bulk RNAseq in HCASMC. Given these findings, we investigated the expressed gene programs in SMC directed by TEAD1 by performing TEAD1 knockdown with siRNA in HCASMC along with bulk RNAseq. The transcriptomic changes with TEAD1 knockdown showed strong enrichment for processes such as ‘cellular response to cAMP, ‘extracellular matrix organization’, ‘connective tissue development”, and ‘chondrocyte development’ (Fig. 5H). These findings are in line with what we observed from our TEAD1 ChIPseq functional enrichment, further corroborating the hypothesis that TEAD1 plays a major role in the smooth muscle transition process to affect the development of phenotypically transitioning SMC.
If the conclusion is that Tcf21 promotes the protective FMC1 and competes with TEAD1 which promotes the CAD-risk-enriched state FMC2, it may be important to know whether TEAD1 acts as an independent disease promoting factor or modulates risk through its interaction with TCF21.
This is an important question, given that the distribution of TEAD1 expression tracks with the FMC-2 population. First, we investigated summary level Million Veteran Program CAD GWAS data at the TEAD1 locus and noted there is a highly significant peak ~300,000 basepairs from the TEAD1 gene. There are no vascular tissue eQTLs among the CAD associated SNPs, but modest eQTLs identified in testis and blood cells point to the closer ARNTL gene. As we have identified numerous examples where a single disease associated enhancer can regulate expression of multiple genes, we cannot rule out the possibility that variation at this locus regulates TEAD1 and has a direct causal effect on CAD risk. This is obviously an important question but studying a primary role for TEAD1 CAD causality at this point would be a substantial genome editing endeavor. We are working on CRISPR screens of CAD loci genes and will build guides to target the enhancers in this locus for these future studies. Also, we hope to address the question whether this gene promotes or inhibits the FMC-2 state, but this is difficult to address in the absence of SMC eQTLs, and without more detailed study of allelic variation at the TEAD1 locus.
Thus, we can only point to the interaction of TEAD1 with TCF21 as a mechanism of CAD risk, however there is now considerable evidence that this interaction is substantial. We now show new data that these proteins physically interact (Co-IP, Results – line 452, Materials and Methods - line 972, Figure 5G), in addition to colocalization across the genome in discrete enhancer regions (ChIP and PLA), and overlapping CAD GWAS loci enrichment (GWASAnalytics), modulate the binding of each other across pseudotime and promote the transcriptional activity of each other (luciferase assays).
Further, in new analyses we provide additional data that TCF21 risk is accentuated through interactions with TEAD1. Employing ChIPseq binding data and GWASAnalytics results for GWAS SNP localization, we found that all TCF21 binding sites, including those with TEAD1 peaks, showed high level enrichment for CAD (-log p-value 10), but in the absence of TEAD1 peaks showed only low-level enrichment for cancer and metabolism (S-Fig. 9F, I). Also, TEAD1 peaks including TCF21 peaks showed strong enrichment for hypertension (-log p-value 10), while TEAD1 peaks only showed low level enrichment of SNPs for diabetes and hypertension (S-Fig. 9G, H). Taken together, these data suggest that the interaction of TCF21 and TEAD1 play a significant specific role toward CAD risk.
These analyses are now included in the Results section of the manuscript.

Bulk RNASeq deconvolution, line 880:
Bulk RNASeq fastq files were downloaded from GSE113348 and processed through a uniform pipeline with cutadapt (5.0), STAR (2.7.10b) and featureCounts (2.0.6) for trimming, alignment and generation of count matrices, respectively. Response to Reviewer Comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have responded to all my questions and I have no further concerns. This will be a nice use of single cell technology to identify cellular trajectories.
We thank the Reviewer for their insightful suggestions during this process.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Li and Kundu and colleagues do an excellent job in responding to all reviewer comments and concerns, have added substantial new genomic and experimental analyses from their own and public data – including elegant spatial data, have performed in vitro SMC functional studies (including clever use of selected human SMC lines of specific molecular phenotype) to validate key new regulators/drivers and SMC-derived cell states, and have revised their model and interpretation of data to reflect more openly the advanced knowledge yet the uncertainties and conflicts in data and possible limitations.
